newsitem.title: CHINA: Shanghai pushes state firms to list indirectly.
newsitem.headline: Shanghai pushes state firms to list indirectly.

text.p: Shanghai is pushing healthy unlisted state firms to buy controlling stakes in poorly-performing listed firms in return for stock exchange listings, officials and analysts said on Monday.

One industry source said the first of the indirect listings is likely to occur by the end of this month, with a national-level state corporation which he refused to name buying a controlling stake in a listed Shanghai firm.
An official with the city's economic planning section confirmed the overall plan, but declined to give details.
"Concrete measures are still under consideration," he said.

Analysts said the plans fit in well with Beijing's desire to get well-run state-enterprises to take over poorly-run state firms and improve their operations as an alternative to wholesale bankruptcies and lay-offs.
"The move is part of a reform to reconstruct state industry and save those poorly-reputed listed firms," said one executive with a major Chinese securities house.

"Some listed companies have lost so much money or have become so unprofitable that they have lost the value of being a listed company. They are unable to give returns of any kind to investors," he said.

Some 43.7 percent of all China's state enterprises were operating in the red in 1996, official figures show. The figures for Shanghai were not available but would only be slightly better, analysts said.
All 563 listed firms on China's stock markets in Shanghai and Shenzhen were originally state-owned firms and the state remains the major shareholder in most of them.

An analyst with a western brokerage in Shanghai said investors would question whether such share purchases were in their best interests, and whether or not there was official pressure behind the deals.
"Something like this could undermine the confidence of the market, foreign investors are not stupid and local investors are less and less naive," the analyst said.

"Many of these firms should be closed, not merged. They should face these problems squarely and not sweep them under the carpet. They don't solve anything by transferring assets of a loss-making firm to one that's profitable," she added.
For unlisted firms, the proposal has some attractions, in spite of the added burden of debt and management responsibility, because of restrictions on gaining share listings in China, analysts said.
Share listings on China's two exchanges, both founded in 1990, are based on a complex quota system with some firms having great trouble in obtaining approval to list.
Stock analysts said a major obstable to the new move could come from listed firms which might not be willing to be taken over.
"Officials in some poorly-managed companies might hope to struggle to survive instead of being dismissed after a merger," one analyst said.
Some listed firms which could be the targets of such take-overs have been the subject of speculative share trading in recent weeks, analysts said.
"Acquisitions and takeovers will become a major speculative topic if the city government can manage to push forward the process," said one trader.
